questions.q: In a standard train/validation/test split, what is the validation set used for?
options: It's what the model directly trains its parameters on
Comparing models, tuning hyperparameters, and deciding when to stop, during development
It is never actually used for anything
Reporting the single final honest performance number
questions.explain: The validation set is checked repeatedly during development to guide decisions like model choice and hyperparameter tuning — distinct from the test set, which is reserved for one final, honest check.

questions.q: Why can't the test set be reused repeatedly for tuning decisions the same way the validation set is?
options: Test sets are always too small to be useful
Repeatedly using it to make decisions leaks information into those decisions, even though the model's gradients never directly trained on it, which makes the final reported number no longer honest
The test set contains different features than the validation set
Test sets can only be used with neural networks
questions.explain: Even though a model doesn't train its parameters on the test set, a human repeatedly adjusting choices based on test performance is effectively 'fitting' to that data too — which is why the test set must be checked only once, after every decision is already finalized.

questions.q: In the scikit-learn GroupKFold example, what happens across the four CV iterations shown?
options: The same fold is held out as the test set in every iteration
A different slice of the data is held out as the test fold each round, and every sample gets held out exactly once across all rounds
No data is ever held out; everything is always used for training
The test set grows larger with each iteration
questions.explain: Cross-validation rotates which fold serves as the held-out test portion across multiple rounds, so every sample gets a turn being evaluated on, and results are averaged across rounds.

questions.q: Why is cross-validation more data-efficient than a single fixed validation split, especially for smaller datasets?
options: It requires collecting additional data beyond what you already have
It never actually evaluates the model
Every sample gets used for both training and evaluation (in different rounds), instead of permanently sacrificing one fixed slice
It eliminates the need for a test set entirely
questions.explain: Rather than permanently setting aside one chunk of data purely for validation, cross-validation rotates the held-out portion across rounds so every sample contributes to both training and evaluation at different points.

questions.q: What is the one rule that, if broken, invalidates a train/validation/test evaluation?
options: The train set must always be larger than the test set
The held-out data (validation or test) must never influence training or decision-making in any way
Validation and test sets must have the same number of rows
Cross-validation must always be used instead of a single split
questions.explain: If held-out data influences feature choices, hyperparameter tuning, or even when to stop training, it is no longer a fair, unbiased check — the final performance number it produces can no longer be trusted as honest.
